PURPOSE: The ledger of chain ids this project has allocated. It is part of the compatibility contract, not a note about it: a second implementation reads it to learn which networks exist and which identity each id was allocated to, spec/chainid_allocation_test.go reads it to refuse a reuse, and this file is EMBEDDED IN EVERY BINARY (spec.CheckChainID) and read again at node startup, so a parameter set that reuses a spent id is refused by the node rather than only by the test suite. Adding a network means adding an entry here in the same commit that adds its parameter file.
RULE: A chain id is allocated once and is never reused. Not by a respin of a network, not by a fork of one. An id that appears below is spent, whatever became of the network that held it. THE ONE EXCEPTION IS BELOW, and it is an exception with preconditions rather than a repeal: where they do not all hold, this rule is the answer.
THE_PRE_MAINNET_RESPIN_EXCEPTION: A network may keep its chain id across a respin when ALL THREE of these hold, and the entry that does it must say so in its 'why'. (1) Mainnet has not launched, so no chain anywhere is load-bearing and nothing of value is denominated on the network being respun or on any network a confusion could reach. (2) The respin MOVES A CONSENSUS VALUE, so the parameter set derives a different consensus root and therefore a different genesis id. (3) The old incarnation is gone -- taken down, not running beside its replacement. WHAT THIS COSTS, stated plainly because it is the whole price: this ledger's protection is against an id handed to a network whose parameter VALUES are identical to a spent one, which is the single case no preimage can separate (see WHY). Precondition 2 is exactly the statement that this respin is NOT that case -- the signing preimage already distinguishes the two incarnations, so the predecessor's certificates fail V2 on the successor even though V1 still passes -- so what is given up here is not the protection this ledger exists to give. What IS given up is real and is this: the startup refusal in spec.CheckChainID no longer fires for this id, because the pin below is moved to the new genesis rather than left pointing at the old one. An operator still running the old parameter file is no longer told by the binary that their network is gone; they are told by the handshake, which refuses a peer whose network id differs, and by the fact that no honest peer serves the old chain. That is a worse error message and not a weaker rule, and it is the trade the preconditions are chosen to make affordable. THE EXCEPTION DOES NOT REACH MAINNET. Chain id 1 fails precondition 1 the moment it is live, and that is the case this rule most needs to keep protecting: once coins are denominated on a chain, an id reused for its replacement puts the predecessor's certificates through V1 on a network where somebody is holding value. A mainnet respin takes a new id, and the general rule above is not negotiable for it.
WHY: The message every certificate signer signs is blake3('zcd/sig/v1' || chain_id_le || consensus_root || cert_body_root) (core/crypto.SigningMessage). It binds the chain id AND the consensus root, which is the digest over every consensus parameter and is the value block 0 carries as its ParentID. Because the preimage carries the consensus root, a network that reuses a spent id does not inherit that network's certificates by default: a respin moves genesis_time, so it derives a different consensus root, and every certificate lifted off the predecessor fails V2 on it even though V1 still passes. What the binding cannot separate is two incarnations whose parameter values are IDENTICAL -- a fork over history rather than over rules, and a same-file reset that wipes a data directory without touching the parameter file. Both derive the same consensus root, so no preimage can tell them apart; that is a property of identity rather than a gap, and for the reset it is wanted, because the reset is meant to be the same network. Only a distinct chain id separates those, and TagSig freezes at block 0 so there is no in-protocol path to change what a signature covers ever again. THAT is what this ledger is for. The peer handshake does not cover it either: Engine.OnHello refuses a peer whose network id differs, but that is a peering rule -- a certificate handed straight to a node's RPC never travels as gossip and never meets a handshake.
WHY_THE_BINDING_IS_NOT_A_SUBSTITUTE_FOR_: Stated separately because it changes what the ledger is claimed to do, not whether it is needed. The binding covers every reuse that moves a parameter value, which is every respin and every rules fork. The ledger covers the remainder -- an id handed to a network whose parameter values are identical to a spent one -- and it covers it at review time and at node startup rather than at V2, which is the only place a case no preimage can distinguish CAN be covered. The two are complementary and neither is redundant with the other.
WHERE_THIS_LEDGER_IS_ENFORCED: Two places, and they check different things. spec/chainid_allocation_test.go binds the parameter files THIS REPOSITORY SHIPS and runs in `go test ./spec`: it is what makes a respin a deliberate line in a diff. spec.CheckChainID runs at NODE STARTUP against whatever parameter set the process resolved -- an embedded one or the file an operator passed to --params -- and refuses two cases the ledger can prove: a chain id whose entry is 'retired', and a chain id whose entry is 'live' while the parameter set in hand derives a different genesis id from the pinned one. That second case is the deployed respin: an operator who edits their copy of params.testnet.json to move genesis_time and keeps chain_id 2 is refused by the binary, without having run any test. `zcd` deliberately does NOT carry the refusal: `zcd genesis --params <file>` is how the genesis id an entry pins is computed in the first place, and a tool that refused to print the number this file is waiting for could never be used to allocate an id or to retire one.
WHAT_THIS_LEDGER_STILL_DOES_NOT_REACH: Three things, all deliberate. (1) An id no entry below allocates is permitted: a private network on a free id is what HOW_TO_ALLOCATE leaves room for, and refusing it would make our node a gate on other people's networks. (2) A 'pre-genesis' or 'ephemeral' entry pins no genesis, so there is nothing for startup to compare -- chain id 1 becomes enforceable the day the freeze flips it to 'live' with its announced genesis id, and 1337 never does, by design. (3) A third party who forks the codebase can delete the check along with everything else; what the check binds is a node running OUR binary, which is the population an operator error comes from. A respin performed by editing a deployed parameter file is refused at startup, because this ledger is embedded and read there. And a certificate lifted onto any such network fails V2 unless its parameter values are identical to the ones it was signed under -- the identical-parameters case the preimage cannot reach is the one this ledger has always been for.
HOW_TO_ALLOCATE: Take the lowest id that appears in no entry below. Add an entry with status 'pre-genesis' and genesis_id null in the same commit as the parameter file. When that network's parameters freeze and it is deployed, flip the status to 'live' and record the genesis id `zcd genesis --params <file>` prints. When it is taken down, flip the status to 'retired' and leave the entry -- a retired entry is the whole point of the ledger, because it is what makes the id unavailable to the network that replaces it.

STATUS_VALUES.pre-genesis: The network's parameters are still moving and its block 0 has never been produced. genesis_id MUST be null: there is nothing to pin, and a pinned value here would be a stale one. Nothing can be replayed off a network that has never run, so the id is reserved and not yet spent.
STATUS_VALUES.live: The network is deployed and its parameters are frozen. genesis_id MUST be recorded, and MUST equal the id the embedded parameter file derives today. This is the pin that catches a respin: a rewritten parameter file that keeps the id produces a different genesis, and the comparison fails.
STATUS_VALUES.retired: The network is gone and its id is spent forever. genesis_id MUST be recorded, and no embedded network may hold this id. Certificates of a retired chain still name its chain id and pass V1 on any successor -- and they pass V2 only on a successor whose parameter values are identical, which is exactly the case this ledger exists to make somebody type out.
STATUS_VALUES.ephemeral: An id reserved for throwaway local networks that are respun freely by design and on which no value is ever held. genesis_id MUST be null, because there is no single genesis to pin. This is a deliberate carve-out from the rule and not an oversight: replaying a certificate from one developer's laptop network onto another's costs nobody anything, and pinning a genesis here would fire on every routine parameter edit and train people to update the ledger without reading it.

allocations.why: The main network. Its parameters are not frozen: they are what the pre-genesis freeze exists to fix, so its genesis id is deliberately unpinned until then. Flipping this entry to 'live' with the announced genesis id is part of the freeze, and is the step that makes id 1 spent.

The public testnet, RESPUN on its genesis_time of 2026-09-04T13:00:00Z and KEEPING chain id 2 under THE_PRE_MAINNET_RESPIN_EXCEPTION. The first incarnation ran from 2026-08-30T00:00:00Z and derived genesis id 0x0c3cdc8b74cd65eae9604f49ee206a952a089b2c025d4f04a90fa38072738935; it is gone, and the pin above now names the successor. All three preconditions hold and are worth checking against the entry rather than trusting: mainnet has not launched, so nothing anywhere is denominated on this chain or reachable from it; the respin moves genesis_time AND the proof-of-work encoding AND the work function itself, so the consensus root moves and the predecessor's certificates fail V2 here rather than being billed; and the first incarnation is taken down rather than running beside this one. WHAT FORCED THE RESPIN: the hashing blob was reshaped so that stock XMRig can mine this chain, which is a consensus change that invalidates every header the old testnet produced -- the old chain could not be continued, only replaced. THE GENESIS ID MOVED A SECOND TIME, BEFORE THIS NETWORK WAS EVER STOOD UP, and the reason is recorded rather than smoothed: pow_engine became randomx-v2 and the header grew a 32-byte field for the commitment work check, both of which are in the consensus root. This network is BORN on rx/2 rather than forking onto it, so there is no third incarnation and no chain was interrupted -- the pin above simply names the parameters that will actually produce block 0. See docs/decisions/randomx-v2.md. The rest of the original entry still holds. This network carries mainnet's consensus rules under an id distinct from mainnet's 1, so a certificate signed for one is refused on the other by V1 and by the signing preimage both.

The throwaway development network. Reset from genesis many times a day on developer machines and in CI, holding no value on any of them. The id is reserved so that no public network is ever given it, which is the part that matters; which particular devnet genesis is running at a given moment is not.
